summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands stands under the full United States federal framework, and that framework sets what a trans visitor faces at the border. United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker was eliminated by executive order in January 2025, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.

Airport screening follows federal procedure. Transportation Security Administration body scanners can flag trans bodies and trigger secondary screening and pat-downs; travellers may request an alternative screening method or decline the scanner. A4TE's airport guidance covers these rights for U.S. nationals arriving in or departing the territory.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

On the territorial layer, the U.S. Virgin Islands human-rights law prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity. In March 2017 the territory's Attorney General issued an official interpretation that this anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, extending territorial protection to a group that has faced exclusion elsewhere in the United States.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in the territory since a 2015 Superior Court ruling held that denial of marriage licences to same-sex couples was unconstitutional; later federal recognition settled the question nationwide, so a married couple's status can be relied on. The historic sodomy statute, applied in the territory since 1957, has been replaced.
tangentialFactors:
Territorial protections rest on a local human-rights statute interpreted by the Attorney General rather than on a body of federal case law specific to the islands, so the practical reach of the anti-discrimination guarantee depends on how territorial agencies and courts apply it. Local reporting in July 2017 documented setbacks for the LGBTQ community alongside grounds for optimism, indicating that the political environment has shifted over time even where the statutory baseline has held.

The U.S. Virgin Islands shares the federal screening, documentation and funding regime that applies across United States jurisdictions, so experiences reported at mainland airports are broadly relevant here, with the difference that arrival often occurs by air through a smaller screening facility.
localsOnly:
Residents of the U.S. Virgin Islands are protected by the territorial human-rights law against discrimination on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, and the March 2017 Attorney General interpretation binds the territory's own reading of that law as applied to transgender students in schools.

Residents hold United States passports and are subject to the same federal document rules and the same federal funding decisions affecting health care, so restrictions on gender-affirming care at federally funded institutions apply to them as well as to visitors.

Same-sex couples have been able to marry in the territory since the 2015 Superior Court ruling, and the resulting marriages are recognised federally.
outOfScopeNotes:
The available sources do not state whether the U.S. Virgin Islands human-rights law carries penalties for discrimination, nor whether any hate-crime statute in the territory explicitly covers anti-trans violence. Enforcement record of the anti-discrimination provision is also not sourced here.

A February 2025 measure attributed to the United States State Department is not substantiated by the sources available for this entry; its content and effect on trans travellers are unresolved.

It is not sourced whether the January 2025 federal funding order on gender-affirming care has been litigated or enjoined with specific effect in the territory, nor whether territorial health facilities not dependent on federal funds offer such care.
